Fixing Dundee Turf: Seams, Edges and Rushed Bases

A lifted seam or a scorched patch on a Dundee lawn gets priced after photos or a short visit, not a number quoted over the phone, since what actually failed underneath, a shifting Candler-sand base, a rushed edge, a low-E window reflection, changes the fix more than the square footage does. Dundee's own Development Services Department, not Polk County, still reviews any permit a larger repair might trigger.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Why a ridge lot's base fails differently than a flatwoods one

A rushed base on a Dundee ridge lot doesn't usually fail the way one does on the flatwoods soil around Kissimmee, where a high water table is the main enemy. Here the problem is more often loose Candler sand working its way up through a base that wasn't compacted in proper lifts, or an edge that was stapled into sand that never held the fastener the way heavier soil would. Both show up the same way eventually, a corner that lifts, a section that feels soft underfoot, but the fix on a ridge lot usually means re-anchoring into a deeper, better-compacted base rather than correcting a drainage problem.

Matching a shock pad's thickness during a patch, not just the infill

A repair to a section of Dundee turf that originally had a shock pad underneath, typically near play equipment, needs a patch built with the same pad thickness restored, not just infill and turf matched by color. Skipping the pad and rebuilding that section like a standard lawn repair leaves a spot that looks right but no longer cushions a fall the way the original build intended. Confirming whether a damaged section sat over a pad before cutting the patch avoids delivering a repair that quietly changes what the surface was actually built to do.

Say you have a lifted 8-ft seam along one side of the yard

Say a five-year-old Dundee lawn has an 8-ft seam lifting along one edge after a summer of hard afternoon storms, with the turf on either side still holding flat. Whether that's a quick re-glue or a sign the base underneath has washed out along that whole edge isn't something to guess at over the phone, since one fix takes an hour and the other means pulling back several feet of turf to rebuild the rock underneath. A few photos of the lifted section, plus its approximate length, are usually enough for a first read; a short site visit confirms it before any number gets quoted.

Storm-season checks after a ridge lot's afternoon downpour

Central Florida's summer storms can drop an inch or more of rain in under an hour, and on an exposed ridge lot without much windbreak, the same storm brings wind gusts that test every staple and glued seam a lawn has. Walking the perimeter after a hard storm, checking specifically for a lifted corner or a seam that's started to peel, catches most repair needs while they're still small enough to re-anchor rather than replace. A lawn that's cleared two or three rainy seasons without a lifted edge has usually proven its anchoring was done right the first time, a pattern covered in more depth here.

An old fines-crusted base undermining a fresh reseam

Reseaming turf over a base that was never washed properly in the first place looks fine on install day, since the new tape and adhesive bond correctly to whatever surface is there. The problem shows up later on a Dundee lawn when that crusted, poorly draining base keeps shifting slightly with every heavy rain, working the fresh seam loose from underneath even though the seam work itself was done correctly. Identifying an unwashed, crusted base during the site visit, rather than after a second failure, is what keeps a repair from becoming a repeat call.

How a live oak root shows itself differently than a settled base

A base that's settled generally produces a broad, shallow dip, while a root working its way under a Dundee lawn tends to heave a narrower ridge that follows a fairly straight line, often tracking back toward the trunk of a nearby tree. The two causes call for different fixes: a settled area gets built back up and recompacted, while a root-heaved section needs the root itself assessed, sometimes with an arborist's input, before deciding whether to reroute the turf's edge or accept that the same spot will need attention again as the root keeps growing.

Matching an older Main Street driveway edge

Where an older lot near Main Street backs turf up to a driveway or walkway poured decades ago, that edge is often the first place a repair call comes from, since the original slab has settled unevenly in a way a newer Woodland Ranch Estates driveway hasn't yet had time to do. A glued edge that was never feathered to match the slab's actual height, rather than a flat, freshly poured one, tends to show a gap or a ridge sooner than the rest of the perimeter. Re-trimming and re-gluing that one transition is usually a smaller job than the lifted edge first suggests, once photos show exactly where the slab has moved.

What a photo can and can't tell us before a visit

A clear, well-lit photo of an open seam or a wrinkle, taken from a few feet back with another shot close up, is usually enough for us to give a Dundee homeowner a preliminary read on scope before scheduling anything. What a photo can't show is the condition of the base underneath, so that first estimate is always a range rather than a firm number, and it can move once someone's actually lifted the turf on site. Sending photos first still saves a visit in the cases where the problem turns out to be smaller than it looked in a phone picture.

Why a patch at a hardscape edge needs its own check-in

A repair seam that falls right where Dundee turf meets a patio, driveway, or fence line is worth checking on its own schedule apart from the rest of a repaired panel, since two different materials moving independently at that boundary can open a gap there before anything else in the repair shows a problem. A quick look at just that few feet of edge, separate from a general glance at the whole yard, catches the specific failure point a repair at this kind of location is actually most likely to develop first.

Questions people ask

Does a Dundee repair need the town's permit if it's just fixing a seam?

Almost never. A seam or edge repair on existing turf typically doesn't rise to the level of Dundee's building permit process, though a repair that involves regrading a larger section or moving drainage is worth a quick call to Development Services to check before starting.

Why would a five-year-old Dundee lawn need a different fix than a brand-new one?

Age changes what's actually wrong more than it changes the diagnosis process. An older lawn's problem is more often infill loss or a base that's finally shown a compaction gap; a newer lawn's issue is more often a single bad seam or edge from the original install, not a wear problem.

What should the best artificial turf repair company near me in Dundee ask before quoting a fix?

Whether they ask for photos and the approximate size of the damaged area before naming a number, and whether they ask what's underneath, ridge sand or an older base, rather than assuming every repair is a simple re-glue. A company that quotes a firm price sight unseen is skipping the step that actually determines the fix.
